doc.title: Joanne Brackeen interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 10, 2001

chapter: Career as a leader and teaching
title: Keeping a band together with multiple players per instrument
summary: She keeps two or three players per instrument who know her vocabulary, such as Ira Coleman and Dion Parsons, so one rehearsal suffices.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: Is it possible to keep a band together these days?

Well you know what you do, or what I do is, you kind of have multiple bands. You find people, maybe two or three people that are really into your music on each instrument. Because people are working in so many different groups and we travel so much, so it’s really great when you’ve got your key people there. But I try to have maybe two people on each instrument, maybe a third. Then if one’s not available, they kind of know the vocabulary. Because outside of that it wouldn’t work. I’m even going to Tel Aviv next week and I’m lucky because Ira Coleman has been working on and off with me for about ten years, and Dion Parsons is new but he’s a friend of Ira’s, so he’s been working with me for about a year. So it’s easy. We call one rehearsal. They already have a good idea of what we might do. And that way, you know, maybe there’s twenty-five tunes, maybe we’re only going to play fifteen but we can decide, and put something new in there. It’s difficult just to get a band and rehearse a set, this, this and, you know.
